newsitem.title: JORDAN: Weapons dispute revives U.N.-Iraq feuding.
newsitem.headline: Weapons dispute revives U.N.-Iraq feuding.

text.p: A bitter row between Iraq and the United Nations over disarming Iraq's weapons of mass destruction has raised the stakes in Baghdad's seven-year feud with the world body.
The dispute over movement and access of U.N. arms inspectors hunting down Iraq's weapons arsenal has led the U.N. Security Council to warn of fresh sanctions against Baghdad.
Iraq, already hurting from a trade embargo imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, has rejected the resolution as unjustified and "poisonous".
Diplomats and analysts say another summer showdown between President Saddam Hussein and the U.N. could be on the cards.
"I would say the mood is confrontation," said an Arab analyst, a veteran monitor of the Iraqi government. "I wouldn't rule out any possible reaction from Baghdad."
He said although the Security Council had dropped U.S. and British proposals for immediate travel bans on all Iraqi officials, the tone of Saturday's resolution was still tough.

It suspended a regular two-monthly review of trade sanctions and expressed its "firm intention...to impose additional measures" on Iraqi officials who hinder weapons inspectors from carrying out their work.
"We are getting used to July being the hottest month of the year, politically. So maybe something is being prepared again," said the Arab analyst.
Frequent stand-offs between Iraq and the coalition of Western powers which defeated it in the 1991 Gulf War have a habit of flaring up in the summer.

Last year a similar row broke out over weapons inspections. In September U.S. warships launched cruise missiles against Iraqi military targets after Saddam sent his forces into autonomous Kurdish areas in northern Iraq.

This time the U.N. says the inspectors, looking for weapons of mass destruction and related material documents, were prevented from searching three sites earlier this month. It says Iraq also interfered with U.N. helicopters flights.

Iraq in turn accused some of the inspectors of spying for the United States, trying to search intelligence headquarters outside their mandate, and committing "flagrant aggression" by entering churches and monasteries.
"The Iraqis say they are cooperating...I'm sure they see this resolution as a declaration of war," said a Western diplomat.
The resolution, although watered down, was the strongest U.N. backing of the weapons inspectors in a long time.

Chief weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus complained in January of feeble support from the Security Council. Iraq has portrayed Britain and the United States as isolated over their tougher line against Baghdad than other council members.
The council, which approved the resolution unanimously despite earlier doubts over Russian and Chinese backing, said on Saturday it would review Iraq's compliance in October.
"I think what France, Russia and China are going to do in the next four months is make sure that the Iraqis don't overreact," said one diplomat.
Relations between Iraq and the weapons inspectors, whose approval is vital to the lifting of sanctions on Iraq, have always been tense and suspicious.
A U.N. deal allowing Baghdad to export $2 billion of oil every six months to buy urgently needed medicine and food has not improved Iraq's regard of the United Nations.
Around half the funds allocated to buy humanitarian goods remain in an escrow account awaiting approval of aid contracts. Iraq accuses the U.N. of arbitrarily blocking the deals.
A diplomat recently back from Baghdad said only 30 percent of the food supplies had so far been delivered.
But while humanitarian goods are held up, money from the sale of Iraqi oil has already been allocated to compensate victims of the 1990-91 conflict and fund the activities of the weapons inspectors.
"Opponents of the deal in Baghdad felt the only reason the United Nations wanted (it) was to get money for its own operations," said the Arab analyst. "Well, maybe they're right."
